issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court may interfere with a finding on whether a minor’s partition suit was beneficial when the lower courts reached it by applying a mistaken legal test.
material_facts: The lower courts treated transactions made before the minor’s birth as incapable of supporting a cause of action for partition.
After the minor’s birth, the defendants denied that properties belonged to the joint family and maintained that they were separate properties, and they also claimed that the family had debts.
The courts below rejected those claims, but did not assess whether the defendants’ conduct after the minor’s birth was adverse to his interests.
The second appellate court found that the suit was beneficial to the minor.
issues.conclusion: The lower courts had misdirected themselves on the relevant issue, so the second appellate court could interfere with their finding; the suit was instituted for the minor’s benefit.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a partition suit is beneficial to a minor depends on whether the coparceners are acting adversely to the minor’s interests. Transactions that predate the minor’s birth do not by themselves settle the matter if, after the minor is born, the defendants use the relevant documents to defeat his rights. A finding reached by misunderstanding that issue may be corrected in second appeal.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from a decision in a suit concerning a minor’s interests.
predicates.lower_courts_used_wrong_test: The lower courts assessed whether the suit benefited the minor by treating the timing of earlier transactions as dispositive rather than considering the defendants’ later conduct toward the minor’s rights.
predicates.defendants_later_asserted_claims_adverse: After the minor’s birth, the defendants asserted claims that, if accepted, would defeat the minor’s rights in property claimed to belong to the joint family.

issues.definition: When a second appeal concerns a minor’s partition suit and the lower courts used the wrong test despite later adverse claims by the defendants, the second appellate court may correct the misdirection and find that the suit was beneficial.

issues.legal_issue: A minor’s death during a partition suit instituted on the minor’s behalf does not prevent the legal representative from continuing the suit if the suit was beneficial when instituted, and a resulting severance in status relates to the institution of the suit.
material_facts: A suit for partition of joint family property was instituted on behalf of a minor coparcener through a next friend.
The minor died while the suit was pending and before the court determined whether the suit benefited him.
The minor’s mother was brought on record as his legal representative and continued the suit.
The court found that the defendants’ conduct made partition beneficial to the minor when the suit was instituted.
issues.conclusion: The suit did not abate; the legal representative was entitled to continue it and obtain a decree upon showing that the suit was beneficial to the minor when instituted. The severance in status took effect from the institution of the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, a coparcener’s unequivocal declaration of an intention to separate, including by filing a partition suit, effects severance in status. The same principle applies where a next friend makes that declaration on behalf of a minor, subject to the court’s determination that the action was beneficial to the minor. The court’s decision recognizes the right arising on institution; it does not create the right. The court relied on Girja Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj and Kawal Nain v. Prabhu Lal, and approved Rangasayi v. Nagarathnamma, Ramsing v. Fakira and Mandliprasad v. Ramcharanlal. It rejected the contrary approach in Chelimi Chetty v. Subbamma, Lalta Prasad v. Sri Mahadeoji Birajman Temple and Hari Singh v. Pritam Singh.

predicates.minor_partition_suit_through_next_friend: A partition suit concerning joint family property was instituted on behalf of a minor coparcener by a next friend.
predicates.minor_died_before_benefit_decision: The minor died while the suit was pending and before the court decided whether instituting it was beneficial to the minor.
predicates.suit_beneficial_when_instituted: The court finds that the suit was beneficial to the minor when it was instituted.

issues.definition: If a minor dies before the court decides the benefit of a partition suit instituted on the minor’s behalf, but the suit was beneficial when instituted, the legal representative may continue it and the severance dates to its institution.

issues.legal_issue: A suit for partition concerns property and does not abate under the rule that a personal action dies with the person.
material_facts: The pending proceeding was a suit for partition of joint family properties.
The minor plaintiff died before the suit was heard and decided.
The defendants argued that the cause of action was personal to the minor and therefore ended on his death.
issues.conclusion: The suit did not abate on the ground that its cause of action was personal to the minor, because a partition suit is a suit relating to property.
issues.legal_principle: The maxim actio personalis moritur cum persona applies to actions for damages for a personal wrong, not to a suit for partition, which concerns property. The court relied on Rangasayi v. Nagarathnamma and Mandliprasad v. Ramcharanlal.

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking partition of property.
predicates.plaintiff_died_before_decision: The plaintiff died before the court heard and decided the suit.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff dies before decision in a suit seeking partition of property, the suit does not abate as a personal action.
